title: Acute agitation management in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder
bottleneck: Agitation in psychosis and mania creates dangerous situations for patients and staff and drives emergency visits, yet available drugs have delayed onset, require injection or restraint-adjacent administration, and carry heavy sedation and metabolic costs. The neurobiology of agitation itself is poorly understood.
why_it_blocks: Agitation is where psychiatric illness meets coercion: poor options mean more restraint, more trauma, and more avoidance of care. Better acute management would reduce both harm and the adversarial character of emergency psychiatry.
current_state: Atypical antipsychotics (often intramuscular) plus benzodiazepines are standard; newer sublingual and inhaled formulations aim for faster, less coercive control. Non-pharmacological de-escalation is recommended but under-resourced. Sublingual dexmedetomidine offers a non-injectable option for acute agitation, but real-world uptake is limited by cost and emergency-department workflow constraints.
